How Sporting™ was born

The official name of the discipline is Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™. Parcours de Chasse is French for «hunting course». Targets move the way real game (the birds and animals people hunt) flies or runs: towards the shooter, away, across, high or low, sometimes between trees. So hunters could practise without shooting a live animal.

Hunters practised like this over natural ground long before any official rules, especially in Great Britain. There the format is called English Sporting, and it has its own rules today. Each club built its course its own way, so scores from different events were hard to compare.

FITASC turned this idea into an international discipline with common rules. FITASC's own documents give two different years. The current rulebook (2025 edition) says 1960 on the cover and 1967 on the last page, and the FITASC history page says 1967. So the honest answer is: it became a FITASC discipline some time in the 1960s.

After that the discipline grew fast. FITASC has held European Championships annually since 1968 and World Championships since 1979. In the USA a related format is known as sporting clays; it is run by the NSCA under rules of its own.

Sporting™ Today's rulebook still says it plainly: the discipline copies hunting situations. You shoot a hunting gun at targets thrown over real countryside. A course is made up of several layouts, and on each layout you shoot 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles (a double is two targets, so 10 more). An international competition is 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 16 · 200 targets in rounds of 25

Sporting™ The hunting roots show in the details. In the ready position the stock (the back part of the gun that goes to the shoulder) touches the body. But its top stays below a line marked on the jacket, 25 cm below the shoulder axis. It looks like the gun of a hunter waiting for a bird. The shooter mounts the gun (brings it up to the shoulder) only once the target has been released and can be seen.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 3 · Ready position: feet and gun

Key points

  • Parcours de Chasse means «hunting course»: targets move like game.
  • Similar shooting existed long before the rules, especially in Great Britain.
  • FITASC documents give 1960 or 1967 as the start; the honest answer is the 1960s.
  • On one layout you shoot 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles (a double is two targets, so 10 more); an international competition is 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25.
  • FITASC has held European Championships annually since 1968 and World Championships since 1979.

Did you know?

The rules of Sporting™ belong to FITASC: the cover says so, next to the year the discipline was created.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. What does Parcours de Chasse mean?

    1. «Shooting range»
    2. «Fast shooting»
    3. «Hunting course»
    Answer

    «Hunting course»

    The name reflects the idea: targets move like game on a hunt.

  2. Which years do FITASC documents give for the start of Sporting™?

    1. 1960 and 1967
    2. 1921 and 1938
    3. 1989 and 1991
    Answer

    1960 and 1967

    The rules give 1960 on the cover and 1967 on the last page, so we say: the 1960s.

  3. How many targets do you shoot on one Sporting™ layout?

    1. 10
    2. 25
    3. 100
    Answer

    25

    On each layout you shoot 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles (a double is two targets, so 10 more).
